title: Pull Requests Reviewers Can Approve Without Guessing
summary: A tidy diff isn't enough. Name the behavior you changed, say why the new way is safer, show evidence and note what stayed the same, so approval isn't a guess.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
A PR lands in the review channel at 4 p.m.: "small fix for checkout validation." Twelve lines changed, CI is green. Three people open it, scroll once, close the tab and wait for someone else to approve first.

Nobody writes "I don't trust this." They write "Can you add a bit more context?" or "What happens if the coupon expires mid-checkout?" or nothing at all. The author sees a slow review. The reviewers see a change they can't size up. Nobody did anything wrong, and the PR still sits there until tomorrow.

The basics (keep it small, write a clear title, read your own diff first) are in the PR writing checklist. This post picks up from there. Once the basics are in place, what makes a reviewer comfortable putting their name on your change?

What reviewers are actually missing

Microsoft researchers asked reviewers directly. They ran a company-wide survey that got 911 responses and sat with four teams for a week each. Reviewers said finding time for every review request was hard. So was understanding the code's purpose, the motivation for the change and how it was implemented (MacLeod et al., Code Reviewing in the Trenches). One interviewee said a good review "has a good description of what the problem was, what the solution is." The paper's advice to authors follows from that: document why you made the change, describe it and how to approach the review, and test it before you send it.

Google's review guide makes the same point from the author's side. A description should say what is changing and why. "Fix bug" doesn't count, because the reader's first questions are which bug and what you did about it (Google Engineering Practices: Writing good CL descriptions).

So most of the hesitation comes from missing information. The reviewer is rebuilding your intent from the diff, the ticket and their memory of the codebase, squeezed between their own tasks. Every piece you hand over up front is one less thing they have to guess. Five pieces cover most PRs.

1. Name the behavior, not the file

"Update CheckoutForm" tells the reviewer where to look. "Reject expired coupons before payment authorization" tells them what the system will do differently. Reviewers don't approve files. They approve a change in behavior, and once they know which one, they read the diff with a goal.

A quick test: write one line in the form "Before this PR, the system did X. After it, the system does Y." If you need three exceptions to finish that line, the PR probably holds more than one change. Splitting it helps you as much as the reviewer.

2. Say why the new way is safer

"Cleaned up the coupon flow" asks the reviewer to take your word for it. Cleaner is a feeling. Safer is an argument they can check. Name what was wrong with the old shape, then point at how the new one fixes it:

Three sentences in the description

"The old flow validated the coupon after creating the payment intent, so an expired coupon could still leave a pending authorization. This PR moves validation before authorization. The payment step itself is unchanged."

Now the reviewer knows which lines carry the risk. They'll still read the whole diff, but with a map in hand.

3. Show evidence where the risk is

Evidence doesn't mean pasting 200 lines of terminal output. It means showing you looked where this change could break:

  • Bug fix: the regression test, plus one line on the case that used to fail.
  • UI change: a screenshot and the screen sizes you checked.
  • Migration: the rollback path and how many rows it touched in staging.
  • Config or flag change: who gets the new behavior and how to turn it off.

This matters most when the diff looks tiny. A one-line condition can change a business rule. A renamed field can break a partner integration. A new default value changes data for every new user. Line count says nothing about blast radius, so don't leave the reviewer to estimate risk from line count. GitHub's docs make a similar point: good context says why the change is needed, what changed and where reviewers should pay special attention (GitHub Docs: Helping others review your changes).

4. Say what didn't change

This one is easy to forget. When a PR touches a sensitive area, reviewers start worrying about the neighbors. Does this change the retry policy? Does it affect existing customers? Does the migration rewrite old orders? One line each settles it: "No change to the retry policy." "Historical orders aren't backfilled in this PR."

It feels redundant to you, because you already know where the change stops. The reviewer doesn't. A boundary note saves them a round of questions and saves you a day of waiting for the answers.

5. Name the trade-off before someone asks

Google's guide lists shortcomings of the approach among the things a description can include. Plenty of us leave them out because it feels like admitting weakness. It works the other way round. "I kept the existing service boundary even though this helper could be shared, because the second consumer isn't confirmed yet" shows the reviewer you saw the alternative and picked one on purpose. They may still disagree, and that's fine. The conversation now starts from your reasoning.

Trust adds up, one PR at a time

Reviewers remember authors whose thinking is easy to follow. After a few PRs with a clear behavior line, real evidence and honest trade-offs, your next PR gets read differently. The reviewer spends their time on the calls that need a second person: design, edge cases, how the change fits next quarter's plans. That's the review you wanted in the first place.

It adds up the other way too. When reviewers can't tell where the risk is, they ask broad questions. Broad questions feel slow, and a little insulting, to the author. Opening a PR starts to feel expensive, so the next one gets bigger, and bigger PRs are harder to trust. A few lines of context break that loop early.

None of this means every PR needs an essay. A two-line copy fix doesn't need a before-and-after section, so match the description to the risk. The description also outlives the review: Google's guide points out that it becomes a permanent part of version control history, and someone will search for it later. There's more on that in your reviewer is the code's first future reader.

Try it on your next PR

  • Put the "before X, after Y" line at the top of the description.
  • Add one sentence on why the new shape is safer than the old one.
  • Attach evidence that matches the risk: a test, a screenshot, a rollback plan.
  • Add one "no change to..." line for the nearest thing a reviewer might worry about.
  • Read the PR as if you were the reviewer. Where would you stop and hesitate? Answer that in the description.

faqs.q: What should a pull request description include?
faqs.a: One line on how behavior changes (before and after), why the new approach is safer, evidence that matches the risk, what stays the same, and any trade-off you made. Google's review guide asks every description to say what changed and why.

faqs.q: Why do reviewers hesitate on a small PR with green CI?
faqs.a: Line count and passing tests don't tell them which behavior changed or where the risk sits. In a Microsoft study, reviewers said understanding a change's purpose and motivation was one of their main struggles. A short description that answers those questions removes most of the hesitation.

faqs.q: How long should a PR description be?
faqs.a: Match it to the risk. A copy fix needs a sentence. A change to payments, permissions or data needs the before-and-after line, the reason, evidence such as a test or rollback plan, and a note on what it does not touch.

faqs.q: Should I mention what my PR does not change?
faqs.a: Yes, for anything a reviewer might reasonably worry about. A line like "No change to the retry policy" takes seconds to write and saves a round of questions.
